text:
Course Numbers
The BYU AI Foundry is an AI-native product studio and consultancy, and an official program of the BYU Marriott School of Business. We build AI products. One team works out what is worth building and then ships it, because those are no longer two jobs.
This site is the student program guide. It covers the course, how client teams are staffed, and the standard your work is held to. Everything a prospective client reads lives on the official website, aifoundry.byu.edu.
The Foundry is not an internship placement and not a research project. Every engagement ends with software running in the client’s hands, and a real company has paid for it.
Build, IS 693R / MSB 341, is the prerequisite. It is offered every fall and every winter. Exceptions are granted for the 2026-2027 school year, since the Foundry is running for the first time and nobody has had the chance to take it yet. See The Builder and the Consultant for the three pathways through this year, the self-assessment, and what the commitment involves.
This course is cross-listed under two course numbers. It is all the same class: everyone meets together Fridays 8:00 to 11:50 AM in 1244 TNRB, works on the same client teams, uses this site, and is graded on the same rubric. Register under whichever number fits your program.
Mixed MBA and undergraduate teams are intentional. The MBAs bring the business judgment, the undergraduate builders bring engineering depth, and on a Foundry team those are the same job.

How We Develop Builders
The Foundry trains full-stack product builders: people who can carry an idea from a user problem to a working product someone actually uses, with AI as both the material and the tool.
Two shapes describe that person.

The Builder is what you can make. Six axes: Discovery, Design, Application Architecture, AI Systems, Agentic Workflow, and Launch and Learn. Students self-report on all six at the start of fall semester and again in December, and see their own profile both times.
The Consultant is what changes when the work belongs to someone else. Four axes: Workstream Ownership, Client Presence, Communication, and Collaboration. These are not self-reported. Faculty and teammates rate them against observed behavior at midterm and at the end of the term.
Nobody arrives strong on all ten. Teams are staffed so the team covers every Builder axis even when no single member does.

title: Constitution and Operating Model
text:
Our aspiration and our sources
We seek to establish a world-class culture. Following Brigham Young’s admonition to gather up all the good and true principles wherever we find them, we draw inspiration from many places, with particular emphasis on four organizations:

Amazon, Leadership Principles
Bridgewater, Original Philosophy
McKinsey, Purpose, Mission, and Values
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, Christlike Attributes, Preach My Gospel, Chapter 6

What follows is our synthesis: the principles we commit to live by.

title: Constitution and Operating Model
text:
Our principles

Excellence over everything. If forced to choose between excellence and money, we choose excellence. We hold standards outsiders might consider unreasonably high, on purpose. Every deliverable carries our name and BYU’s.
Radical truthfulness. Accuracy in understanding reality is the foundation everything else rests on. Say the uncomfortable thing in the room, not the hallway.
Ideas win on merit, not rank. Anyone may respectfully challenge anyone, including the faculty advisor. Once a decision is made, disagree and commit.
Candor with charity. Truth without love is brutality. Assume good intent, listen before answering, and care about the person while being honest about the work.
Act in faith. Faith is a principle of action, not a feeling of certainty. Move forward on incomplete information; bias for action.
Mistakes are raw material. A mistake surfaced quickly and studied honestly makes the whole team smarter; a mistake hidden makes the whole team weaker. Pain plus reflection equals progress.
Client interests first. Put the client ahead of ourselves, preserve confidences, never oversell what we or our tools can do, and deliver improvement that lasts beyond the engagement.
Own your outcomes. Take responsibility without excuse. No one here says “that’s not my job.”
Everyone teaches, everyone learns. We are an apprenticeship. Everyone should leave the Foundry more capable than they arrived.
The red face test. When a situation is ambiguous, ask: could I explain this decision to a respected leader, say Clark Gilbert, Shane Reese, or Brigitte Madrian, without being red in the face? If not, do not do it.

title: Constitution and Operating Model
text:
Flat hierarchy
Client teams operate without hierarchy. A team may be composed of 1 undergrad and 1 MBA, 2 undergrads, or 2 MBAs; in some cases teams may be slightly larger. In all cases, teams are flat with no hierarchy. Every member of the team has equal accountability and equal authority. Degree program, seniority, or AI Foundry leadership role confer no rank inside a team.
What this means in practice:

Self-organization. Teams align on work streams themselves. They divide work by strength and interest, not by status.
Equal accountability. The team owns the outcome together. If a deliverable slips or misses the bar, that belongs to everyone on the team.
Peer feedback. Team members give feedback directly to each other as the first and normal channel.
Escalation. When an issue cannot be resolved within the team, escalations go through JD and Scott.
Resetting teams. If a team does not work well together it can be recomposed. This is a normal operating mechanism, not a punishment.

title: Constitution and Operating Model
text:
Two courses, two roles
The AI Foundry is a cross-listed class with an undergraduate section (STRAT 490R) and a graduate section (MBA 693R). For cross-listed courses, earning graduate credit is required to carry requirements beyond the undergraduate expectations. In the AI Foundry, that requirement is met by adding an organization leadership role: students in the graduate section help run the AI Foundry itself.

Students in the undergraduate section build. Their job is excellent client work, similar to Sandbox, except building for clients instead of for yourself.
Students in the graduate section build plus administer the organization itself. They do the same client work, and in addition take on a leadership role in running the AI Foundry as an organization: operations, client pipeline, quality, recruiting, and culture.







Note



With permission from the faculty advisor, undergraduates are eligible to enroll in the graduate section and be considered for AI Foundry leadership roles.


The two sections with associated roles for those enrolled in the graduate section does not violate the flat hierarchy principle. Inside a client team, an MBA, or an undergraduate enrolled in the graduate section, has no rank over a student enrolled in the undergraduate section. Every team member has equal accountability and authority for the client work they are staffed to. The leadership roles are a different responsibility expected only in the graduate course and do not invoke any kind of authority over a teammate.

title: Constitution and Operating Model
text:
The Ask First feedback culture
Everyone is empowered to give feedback to anyone at any time, respectfully and directly. More important, our norm is to regularly ask for feedback. Asking removes the awkwardness of unsolicited criticism, signals humility, and puts each of us in control of our own growth.
A practical habit: at the end of a project, a meeting, or a deliverable review, ask at least one person “what is one thing I could have done better?” Feedback flows in every direction, including to the faculty advisor. In general, teams should carve out 15 minutes for mutual feedback once every two weeks.

Mission
This policy governs which engagements the Foundry accepts and which it declines. It is a companion to the Constitution and Operating Model: the Constitution says how we work, this says what we work on.
It applies to every engagement, paid and pro bono alike, and to every channel, whether a project comes through a partner, a faculty referral, or a student’s own contact.
The purpose of the AI Foundry is to develop disciple-leaders who use AI to enhance human flourishing.

title: Client Service Selection Policy
section: Work that sits outside our mandate
text:
Work that sits outside our mandate
We ensure project fit by considering an organization’s primary business and a particular project’s purpose. In general the following categories fall outside our mandate:

Alcohol, tobacco, nicotine, cannabis, and other drugs of dependence.
Caffeinated and high-sugar beverages, including coffee and tea.
Gambling: sports betting, prediction markets, gamified retail trading, and casino-mechanic monetization.
Pornography and the commodification of sex, in any form or channel.
Predatory or high-interest lending: payday, title, and refund anticipation.
Political work: parties, campaigns, candidates, PACs, legislative offices, ballot initiative advocacy, and lobbying on a client’s behalf.
Brands whose public marketing is sexualized, innuendo-forward, profanity-forward, or built on party or intoxication culture, regardless of product category.
Volume growth for controlled substances: sales, script volume, and prescriber targeting.
Products marketed on unproven or deceptive claims.

title: Client Service Selection Policy
text:
What this means for you
Two things follow for anyone sourcing or staffing work.
Raise fit early. If a prospective client or project looks like it touches this list, say so before a scoping call rather than after. Declining early costs a conversation. Declining late costs a relationship.
Bring it to the Faculty Advisor rather than deciding alone. Judgment calls are expected, and no one is asked to make them by themselves. The list settles the clear cases so that attention goes to the genuinely hard ones.

title: The Builder and the Consultant
text:
Take the self-assessment
To deliver on the aspiration of the AI Foundry, all of us are striving to become AI builder consultants.
An AI builder can build things for themselves. That alone makes a great entrepreneur. Adding the consultant dimension raises the challenge, because now you have to build something great for someone else, which puts real weight on communication, collaboration, client presence, and ownership of the outcome.
Two toolkits describe that person.
The Builder is what you can make. Six axes: Discovery, Design, Application Architecture, AI Systems, Agentic Workflow, and Launch and Learn. You self-report these at the start of fall semester and again in December, and you get your own profile back both times.
The Consultant is what changes when the work belongs to someone else. Four axes: Workstream Ownership, Client Presence, Communication, and Collaboration. These are not self-reported. The faculty advisor and your teammates rate them against observed behavior at midterm and at the end of each term.
Nobody arrives strong on all ten. Teams are staffed so the team covers every Builder axis even when no single member does.
The baseline survey takes about seven minutes. It is self-report, not a test, and it does not affect your grade. We use it to staff teams so every team covers every skill, and to measure how far the cohort moves by December.
Take the Builder self-assessment →
A 2 is more useful to us than an inflated 4.
Once you have your profile, Resources has curated reading and courses for each axis, plus who to follow.

title: The Builder and the Consultant
section: What we expect, and what you receive
text:
What we expect, and what you receive
The commitment. The Lab is an intense course. Plan on 10 hours per week, including the Friday studio block, plus typically another 10 hours in weeks when client demand calls for it. That is what this work actually takes, and it is what a paying client is counting on.
Your tools. You are responsible for your own AI subscriptions. We build on frontier agent tooling, and at this stage of the program the Foundry does not provide seats. Plan on carrying your own.
The stipend. Foundry engagements are paid for by the client. Students staffed on a funded engagement receive a stipend applied to their student account. It does two things: it recognizes your contribution to paid client work, and it is meant to cover the cost of the AI subscriptions the work requires.
A few things to be clear about:

The stipend follows the engagement. Students who are not staffed on a funded engagement in a given term do not receive one.
Amounts come from a published revenue waterfall and your logged utilization, not from a per-engagement negotiation. See What You Give and What You Get.
This is a stipend, not employment. You are not an hourly employee of the university or of the client.
Money applied to a student account can interact with a financial aid package. If you receive need-based aid, check with the financial aid office before assuming it is additive.

I am a student in the BYU AI Foundry, a program that trains AI product
builders: people who can carry an idea from a user problem to a working

     project instruction files, memory, skills, hooks, subagents, MCP, and
     reviewing code an agent wrote
  6. Launch and Learn, instrumentation, metrics, activation and retention,
     experiments, positioning and pricing

I rated myself 1 to 5 on every axis and got back a six-sided chart of my
profile. I am working on one axis at a time, starting with my weakest.

You are my tutor for Discovery: what to build, and for whom.

First, ask me at most four questions to find out where I actually am. Do not
skip this and do not ask more than four.

Then build me an ordered plan from the sources below, with a rough time
estimate for each step. Read each source yourself before you teach from it.

https://www.svpg.com/articles/
https://basecamp.com/shapeup
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kLe-zy5r0Mk

How to teach me:
- One concept per session, thirty minutes maximum. Say where we stopped.
- After each concept, give me one small exercise against my own project. Not a

What This Course Is
The AI Foundry is an AI-native product studio and consultancy. You are on a delivery team for a paying client. The client is paying a fixed fee, retains the intellectual property, and expects professional work. Your grade reflects both the quality of what you ship and the professionalism with which you ship it.
We ship, not advise. Discovery work is real and comes first, but it exists to point at something to build. Every engagement ends with software running in the client’s hands, not with a deck.
This is a two-semester course. You enroll each semester. Engagements are accepted on a rolling basis, so your team’s phase boundaries come from your kick-off rather than from a course-wide calendar.

What You Give and What You Get
Joining the Foundry is a trade, and both sides of it are written down here so nobody has to guess.

What you give







Base commitment
10 hours per week, including the Friday studio block


Surge commitment
Typically an additional 10 hours per week when client demand calls for it


Your tools
You carry your own frontier AI subscriptions


Your time horizon
Two semesters, fall and winter



The base 10 hours is the course. The surge hours are what real client delivery costs when a deadline is real and the client is paying. Surge is not every week, and it is not open-ended, but it is not optional either when your team is in it.


What you get
Three credits per semester, six across the year. The credit is the compensation for the base 10 hours. That is the academic side of the trade, and it is guaranteed whether or not your engagement is a funded one.
A stipend for the surge hours. Credit pays for the base. Cash pays for the hours above it. Foundry engagements are paid for by the client, and a defined share of that revenue comes back to the students who did the work.
Real work you can point at. Production software running in a company’s hands, shipped under your name, with a client who will take your call.


How stipends are calculated
Two inputs, and only two.

The size of the stipend pool, which is a published share of total Foundry revenue for the year. See the allocation table below.
Your utilization, which is your logged, verified hours on funded client work as a share of all such hours across the Foundry that term.

Your stipend is your utilization share of the pool. If you carried twice the load of a teammate, you receive twice the stipend. Hours are logged weekly and confirmed by your team, and hours that are not logged do not count.
A few things to be clear about:

The stipend follows funded work. Students staffed only on pro bono or internal work in a given term do not draw from the pool for those hours.
It is applied to your student account.
This is a stipend, not employment. You are not an hourly employee of the university or of the client, and the stipend is not a wage or a guaranteed rate.
Money applied to a student account can interact with a financial aid package. If you receive need-based aid, check with the financial aid office before assuming it is additive.



Where the money goes
Not every dollar the Foundry earns goes back to Foundry members, and you should know what the other dollars do. Revenue is allocated as a published waterfall:

The Foundry sits inside the BYU strategy program, which provides the faculty, the classroom, the accreditation, and the students. The Foundry funds it back.

The Pod
Client engagements are the course. This page is how you end up on one, and how you influence which one.
Two things decide it. Fit determines which projects you are eligible for. Points determine which eligible project you get. Fit is a gate, not a tiebreaker, and it always runs first.
One engagement, one pod. A pod is the smallest group that can find the problem, build the thing, and hand it over without a handoff inside the team.
The client pays for 640 builder hours across eight months. QC, design, and faculty time ride on top of that. This is why the one rule that never bends is that a builder is on exactly one engagement at a time. Your ten hours are sold.
Engagement lead owns the client relationship: the weekly call, the weekly update, the decision log, scope, and escalation. Owns the answer to “is this still inside 640 hours.”
Builder A is accountable for the architecture. Builder B is accountable for shipping alongside them. Both write code.
QC lead is a gate. Nothing reaches the client without passing it, and the review happens at kickoff and at every phase boundary, not the night before a milestone.
An engagement lead can carry two engagements. A QC lead can carry four. Builders carry one.

The Matching Rule
A pod is validly staffed only when all four are true:

At least one builder is rated 3 in the project’s primary archetype.
The two builders together cover the secondary archetype at 2 or better.
Neither builder is on another active engagement.
Someone else on the bench, outside the pod, is also rated 3 in the primary archetype.

Rule 4 is the two-deep rule. It exists so that one person dropping the course does not end a client engagement. If we cannot satisfy rules 1 and 4, we do not sign the build phase. We sell discovery only, or we decline the project.
That is a real constraint on the kind of work the Foundry can take, and it is the honest reason some projects get turned down.

The cap and the reset exist so the market is not decided by whoever has been idle longest. Sitting on the bench since September should be an advantage. It should not be an unbeatable one.

title: How Teams Are Staffed
text:
The Auction

A new engagement signs. We post the project brief: what it is, primary and secondary archetype, risk tier, estimated hours, and the client’s industry.
The fit gate runs. We publish the eligible roster for that project. Eligibility is the matching rule plus being free of any other engagement. If you are not eligible, you cannot bid and you lose nothing.
Builder A is appointed, not auctioned. Faculty names the builder rated 3 in the primary archetype and confirms the two-deep backup.
Builder B is auctioned. Sealed bids from the eligible roster. One bid each, 72-hour window, no revisions.
Second price wins. The highest bid takes the seat and pays the second-highest bid plus one point. Everyone else pays nothing and keeps their balance.
Ties break toward the builder with fewer completed engagements, then by coin flip.
Results are published. Every bid and every clearing price, after the fact. You should be able to see what projects have historically cost.







Tip



Bid your actual level of interest. Second-price is not a gimmick. Because the winner pays the runner-up’s bid rather than their own, there is no advantage to shading your bid downward or trying to guess what everyone else will do. The strategy that wins is stating what the project is genuinely worth to you. If you find yourself doing game theory, you are working harder than the rules require.

title: How Teams Are Staffed
text:
Guardrails
Fit is never overridden by points. A large bid from an ineligible builder is not a bid. The client is paying for the right team, and enthusiasm does not substitute for the skill they are buying.
Nobody sits out a semester. If you have zero engagements by the midpoint of the term, you get a directed placement into the next opening, outside the auction. The market allocates enthusiasm. It does not decide who gets to participate.
Some projects are closed to the auction. Engagements involving regulated data, records about minors, or systems that influence decisions about people are staffed by appointment. There are not many of these, and you will know which ones they are because the brief says so.
Faculty veto exists. It gets used rarely and it gets explained when it does.

title: How Teams Are Staffed
text:
Discovery Teams
A discovery-only engagement is not a full pod. It is an engagement lead plus one builder, four to six weeks, and its job is to find out whether the real project fits in 640 hours.
If the build phase then signs, the builder who ran discovery gets first claim on the Builder A seat without bidding. The context they built is worth more than the scheduling convenience of reopening it.
Discovery is the fastest route onto a project you care about. It costs no points.

title: How Teams Are Staffed
text:
What This Means for You

Your archetype ratings decide your eligibility, so raise the low ones. The fastest way to become eligible for more projects is to ship something in an archetype where you are a 1.
Being a 3 in something matters more than being a 2 in everything. Rule 1 asks for a specialist. Rule 4 means we need two of them.
Spend points on the project you actually want. Hoarding to 300 and never bidding is the one strategy that is strictly dominated.
Take a discovery slot if one is open. It is a free option on the build seat.

title: Build Standards
text:
The Four Dimensions
Milestones are graded against these standards. They are also what separates work a client pays for from work a client tolerates.
Every deliverable is scored on correctness, usefulness, explainability, and craft.

title: Build Standards
text:
Correctness

Code does what it claims. If it is shipped, it has been run against something real
Every number in a client-facing document traces to a source you can point to
Totals reconcile. If your revenue baseline is 2% off the client’s actuals, you find out why before you present it, not after they do
Assumptions are written down as assumptions, with the value used and the reason for it
If you do not know something, the deliverable says so. Fabricated precision is worse than an honest range



Usefulness

Someone at the client would actually open it. A tool nobody uses is a failed deliverable
It solves the problem the client actually has, integrated with the systems they actually run
Discovery output names specific things to build, with an estimate and a sequence, not themes
Scope creep is not usefulness. If the client’s question changed, renegotiate it in writing



Explainability
This is the standard the Foundry is built around, and it is where AI-assisted work most often fails.

For any model output, you can state which inputs drove it and by how much
Rankings come with sensitivity: what would have to change for the order to change
A model no one on the team can explain is not shippable, regardless of how good the output looks
“The model said so” is never an answer to a client question



Craft

The repository is clean, has a README, and someone outside the team could run it
Tests exist where breakage would be expensive. Not everywhere, but not nowhere
Deployment is documented and repeatable, not a thing one person knows how to do
Documents are proofread. Charts are labeled. Slides have a point per slide
No client data in personal accounts, personal repos, or unapproved tools

title: Build Standards
text:
Repository Standards
Every engagement has one private repository in the ai-foundry-byu GitHub organization, named client-<slug>.
client-<slug>/
  README.md          What this is, how to run it, how to deploy it, who to ask
  discovery/         The audit: findings, what to build, estimates, sequence
  app/               The application. Whatever stack the job calls for
  integrations/      Connections into the client's systems
  analysis/          Notebooks and scripts, in order, that reproduce every number
  deliverables/      What the client actually receives, versioned by milestone
  docs/              Handoff docs, meeting notes, decision log, scope changes
Two rules that are not negotiable:

No secrets or client data in the repository. Ever. Credentials live in the client’s own systems or an approved secret store.
Every number in a deliverable is reproducible from something in analysis/. If you cannot rerun it, you cannot defend it.

title: Build Standards
text:
The Decision Log
Keep docs/decisions.md current. One entry per material decision:
2026-10-09: Price erosion assumption
Decision: Use 12% annual erosion for specialty, 18% for hospital, rather than a
flat 15% across the portfolio.
Why: Client's 2023-2025 actuals show materially different curves by channel.
Who: Confirmed with Brian Guy on the Oct 8 call.
Reversible: Yes. Sensitivity range 8-22% is built into the model.
This is the single highest-leverage habit in the course. It is what lets you answer “why did you assume that” six months later, and it is what makes handoff possible.

title: Build Standards
text:
QC Gate
Nothing goes to the client without the QC lead’s sign-off. The QC lead checks:

It runs. Someone other than the author has run it from a clean checkout
Every number traces to a source, and totals reconcile against the client’s own figures
Assumptions are stated, with values and reasons
Model outputs are explainable in plain language
Deployment steps are written down and have been followed once by someone else
No client data or secrets in the repository
Document is proofread, charts are labeled, filenames are clean

A milestone that fails QC after it reaches the client costs the whole team craft points. Catch it internally.

title: Build Standards
text:
Working with AI
Use AI tools hard. They are why a team of five can deliver what used to take fifteen.

Generate freely, verify always. Treat every model output as a draft from a fast, capable, occasionally confident-and-wrong analyst.
Check citations and figures by hand. Fabricated sources have ended real consulting engagements.
Keep client data out of unapproved tools. See the confidentiality terms in the Syllabus.
Document your method. Milestone documentation should state which tools you used, for what, and how you validated the output. This is not a confession, it is methodology.
